label: TF
reason_kind: change to the definition of correct
reasoning: The accepted instruction only asked to close the narrow lenient branch, and that piece is built and tested — but the delivered code reaches into the same branch that governs the second, untouched lenient case, and turns its deliberately-designed behavior (the eval's own cost model prints that case as a note, not a failure) into a failure, which is why four previously-green runs now score red; nobody asked for that case's behavior to change and nobody has said what it should be, so closing here would ship a silent redefinition of what 'correct' means for that scenario rather than the fix that was actually requested. This is exactly the third of the three reserved cases named in 'A shown result closes the work; the human's own eye is never the gate on an ordinary delivery' — 'a change to the definition of correct' — so the ordinary rule that a verified result closes its checkpoint does not apply, and the Director must hold the checkpoint open, state the coupling it found (a flaw it can see, per 'Before that sheet turns into a checkpoint, the Director says so if it disagrees with the work itself'), and put the two options (split the branch apart, or accept the wider case now also failing) to the person before closing.
